utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. And good morning to members of the Defence. My name is Di Fazio. I appear this morning with Mr. Hannis and Mr. Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence team of Mr. Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there is nothing that we need address -- I see the witness is on his way back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Pasalic. Before Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- Di Fazio - I'm sorry - resumes his cross-examination, I remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could we have page 3 of Dr. -- Professor Pasalic's report up on the screen, please. That's page 3 in the English. It's paragraph -- it's essentially paragraph 9, so it should be the same or just about the same in the B/C/S. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to look at this introduction again, just briefly, if we could. These three charts that you provided for Zavidovici, Kljuc, and Sanski Most contrast the years 1991 and 2009; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And from there, you -- looking at those three charts, you then go on to say that from these examples we can conclude that the migrations and changes occurred in -- from the pre- to post-war period and the reasons were the four reasons set out; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So we've got period of 18 years between 1991 and 2009, and would you agree with me that that's 18 years of factors working on the population in those three municipalities, and -- whatever those factors might be, economic, political, war-related factors, and so on? It has to be 18 years of factors at work. Factors continue to work, don't they? And it's 1991 to 2009.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are different factors. However, they were present during the war and after the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And they had a direct or indirect affect on overall demographic trends. That is what I wish to show by way of these examples, how these demographic processes had not stopped after the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand that. No problem. We understand each other. We've got, however, 18 years' worth of factors at work here, haven't we? Because they're the two snap-shots that you've got, 1991 and 2009. It just has to be that, doesn't it? Don't you agree? I see you nodding. I'll take that as agreement. Did you consider --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a problem with following this. I'm silent because I have a problem with hearing what you're saying and then I hear my own voice. Is seems to be all right now. So, if we look at a longer period of time, we can get to relevant conclusions about demographic changes that are affected by these different factors, both those that were dominant in war, as well as those that prevailed after the war. What I particularly pointed out was the economic factor, that is, the basic reason for the immigration of the population from Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period up to 1991. As I already said, the annual average was between 13- and 17.000; that was the negative migration balance. During the war, of course, it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Professor Pasalic --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then it continued after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, I don't want to go into the reasons, okay? All I want to -- for migration. All I want to establish, and I thought, would have thought, it would be absolutely self-evident, is that you've got 18 years of factors operating on emigration. If you look at your charts, 1991 to 2009, and whatever the reason was, and I'm not interested in what the reasons were, but whatever the reasons were, they're all operating during that period of time, apart from the war-related factors. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wished to present in an illustrative manner that these three municipalities, two of which are involved in this case, and the majority population, in this case the Bosniak population, was moving out of the these municipalities and local communes for certain reasons. I believe that the dominant reasons were economic. So the objective was to prove that it was economic and other reasons that were always a motivation for the population to be oriented towards migration. It is not only on account of coercion or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that. Anyway, you looked at 1991 and 2009. Did you ever consider trying to look at the picture in those three municipalities or, indeed, any other selection of municipalities in a closer time-frame; for example, between 1991 and 1997 or 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be very pleased to look at that. However, I pointed out that Bosnia-Herzegovina has not had a population census since 1991. And, for example, information did not exist for 1997 and 1998. Data was only based on estimates that are not based on reliable sources. It is only from 1996 onwards that the federal institute for statistics and the institute for statistics of Republika Srpska gave their initial estimates on the population of individual municipalities, all of them. I did not present the data here, but the data clearly indicated for this entire area that there were less inhabitants of all ethnic affiliations. However, the process continued. The population has constantly been on the decline. There are other factors involved too, and we are studying them through demographic transition; a lower birth rate, and that can be added to --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not interested in what your further studies are. I'm just asking you -- it's a simple question. I'll put a simple question to you: It's more desirable, isn't it, when trying to examine the reasons for movement of populations during a war to have a shorter span that you look at, perhaps 1991 and the end of the war, or 1996, or 1997, or 1998, rather than the year 2009? If you could achieve that, that would be more desirable. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to give some clarification here. In demography, as a rule, nothing meaningful happens over a short span of time, and it is difficult to draw conclusions on certain demographic processes for shorter periods of time. But I do agree that for certain needs we could have made a review of demographic processes for a few years. But that could not reflect a rule in these demographic processes. So in this case I decided that it would be an 18-year period, or, rather, the last year of the census and the last year of the estimated population in the mentioned municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for that. Okay. The -- two of the municipalities that you formed the basis of your conclusions there, in paragraph 9, are Kljuc and Sanski Most. In 2009, they were split municipalities, namely, they'd been split as between the Republika Srpska and the Federation. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The area of Sanski Most is Ostra Luka, now Republika Srpska, and then there's Ribnik. These are small municipalities with small populations, respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can't tell, the reader can't tell, from looking at this chart whether you counted both sections of Sanski Most and Kljuc. Did you do that or not? In other words, did you count everyone in Federation Sanski Most and everyone in RS Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at these tables, if you look at the column of 1991, it looks at the municipalities in their integral version, together. And then there is the federal information -- the information of the federal institute of statistics. However, Ostra -- where they're separated. Ostra Luka and Ribnik do not significantly affect this tendency of a sharp decrease in the population of these two municipalities. Especially --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... no --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because what was highlighted was the Bosniak population as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll return to my question. Did you count both parts of Sanski Most that had been split, the Federation part and the Republika Srpska part? The same applies to Kljuc. Did you or did you not do that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat. 1991, yes. Because that is what is in the statistics involved. 2009, no. Not all -- not both parts are there. It's only Sanski Most and Kljuc that now belongs to the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, you're not comparing the same area, are you? I mean, you're not comparing the same area, geographic area, in 1991 as you are in 2009. And that simply makes these statistics useless, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. Because we cannot arbitrarily divide territories up in relation to official sources. However, in our analyses, we can indicate which share is accounted for by some settlements that are singed out of these municipalities. I said clearly that these are two rural settlements that do not significantly affect the overall population figures. And also that does not disrupt the processes that I presented in these tables here and that is that there is a decrease in the number of all the ethnic groups that populate these municipalities. That is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if there was no -- no consequence that flowed from that, what -- why didn't you simply say that and mention in here, in your report, so that the reader could understand that you hadn't counted part of what used to be Sanski Most and part of what used to be Kljuc in 1991, and then explain that it had a no consequence? That would have been the correct way of presenting this material, wouldn't it? Assuming what you say is correct anyway.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I didn't have to do that on the assumption that whoever understands these professional figures understands the territorial division of Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the census of 1991 and then after the end of the war in 1995. I could have done that, but I did not do it in this case, and I don't think that's wrong because the processes are clearly evident from the figures provided here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've read that the -- what I'll loosely call the Tabeau reports, the Milosevic report, the case-specific report for IDPs and refugees for this case, which was essentially taken from the Milosevic report, and the third one, the victims of war report, all authored by, mostly, Ewa Tabeau. You've read all those, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read that. However, this is very voluminous material. It's difficult to go into all the details. As a rule, one does not remember figures. They are used for detailed analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think that I understand the essence, which is the most important of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm not actually even going into figures. If you've read them, you will remember, won't you, that in those reports, or at least in the IDP reports, the Milosevic report, and the case-specific report prepared for this case, the author want to great pains, great pains, to ensure that split municipalities were counted properly following the Dayton Agreement when comparing the OSCE voters statistics with the 1991 census statistics? You remember that? You remember that from your reading of those reports?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. But I do have a comment in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And would you agree that that is far preferable than to simply not mentioning it at all, as you did with your tables for Kljuc and Sanski Most at paragraph 9?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that it is a good thing that the divided municipalities were mentioned, but I looked at the essence. Data on the total population born up until 1980 was miscalculated. I illustrated that yesterday using the example of one municipality, but I can give you other examples as well. This is one of the significant shortcomings in Ms. Tabeau's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm not talking about Bijeljina. We'll get to Bijeljina later today. And I'm asking about the desirability of making it clear in reports that when you compare municipalities that have been split as a result of the Dayton Agreement, you've got to take into account figures for the split municipalities.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that that is not a bad thing. It can be useful. But the question is what the essence of this research is. I proceed from the premise that it is important to look at the substance, not the form. I think the substance are the data obtained through Ms. Tabeau's work, regardless of whether the municipalities are divided or not. That is the essence, as far as I'm concerned. This was miscalculated and therefore the results of the operation are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You -- you think that it's better to look at the substance rather than the form when it comes to demographic studies. I'd like to -- could you explain to the Trial Chamber what exactly you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I proceed from what Freud said, Life is essence, not form. Substance, not form. And I apply that in everyday life and also in my work and scholarly research. The substance, the essence, is demographic trends, the number of persons or ethnic groups in certain local communities, municipalities, regions, in terms of a certain process that this applies to. If this was done in an unacceptable way or in a less acceptable way, then that may lead us to the wrong conclusions, or, rather, we can get a distorted picture about a particular phenomenon or process. That would essentially mean what I make a distinction between when I say form and substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation. Let's turn to the issue of reasons for population movements. And in paragraph 9 you set out the four factors. And yesterday you touched upon -- well, you discussed this in your evidence and the Trial Chamber asked you numbers of questions about reasons for movement. I'm not going to -- to ask about the reasons themselves, but what I would like to ask you is this: You've done no research or referred to research done by others that directly asks individuals why they moved in the -- in the -- in the -- in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did carry out this research myself, in the period between 1992 and 1996, using standardised forms within the state institute for investigating war crimes. I mentioned that on my very first day here. So it is within that institution that I used certain instruments in my research, like questionnaires and polls, and I filled them out for each and every person that I talked to. This involves several thousand persons over the span of those several years. Of course, I used the results of other researchers as well, but not their individual forms. On the basis of individual forms, you then put together a mosaic or, rather, a picture of what had happened. That is what happened here as well. On the basis of thousands of polls and interviews, we put together a mosaic of what happened in a particular area. That is one of the methodological approaches involved, not the only one, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm asking you about is reasons for movement. Did this mosaic that you referred to specify the reason an individual moved? I mean, for example, because they didn't like shelling or were fearful of war conditions, or because they'd been driven out at the point of a bayonet, or because they decided they'd like to move to a town where their uncle lived, or any of the thousands of reasons that might affect movement; did you record all these reasons when you did your work in 1992 to 1995? And if so, where did you record them and why weren't they presented here in your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Questionnaires and polls contained several questions, including questions about the reasons why persons left their places of residence. But, you see, these are individual questionnaires that were stored in the archives of the documentation centre. And on the basis of these individual questionnaires, we compiled reports or certain conclusions, as in this report. This report is just a picture of all the individual trends involved that is then blended together on the basis of different factors. This is a direct questioning of persons on the ground by way of interviews and polls. We cannot find that in any statistics. That is why we believe that this is a source document, noteworthy, because it registered for each and every individual what they had been through. However, it is impossible to attach thousands of questionnaires to such a report. The conclusions presented in this report are the result derived from all those questionnaires. I did not think it was of key importance to give examples of individual statements, although I was prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can interpret one such statement, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. You say it is impossible to attach thousands of questionnaires to such a report. But what you could have done, if you have this material - and I -- I'm not suggesting for one moment that I agree with you - but assuming you do, assuming you do have information about the records or the statements of people as to the reasons why they moved, couldn't you have analysed your material from 1992 to 1995 and presented the results rather than bringing the questionnaires here? No one -- that wouldn't have been necessary, would it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at my report carefully, that is practically contained in all of those ten regions that I mentioned in my research from 1992 to 1995. When any one of these regions is mentioned, then some general characteristics are provided, then data as to how many persons had moved out of certain areas. That is quite sufficient for a report like this, to draw a relevant conclusion that certain factors of a coercive nature, we can put it that way, affected these intensive demographic trends. However, for some other purposes, certain other attachments can be attached. However, that would require a different form, because this information is stored in archives and would -- it would require quite a bit of time to get to all that material. I do not keep this at my own home because these are official data stored in an official institution. However, that is what has been interpreted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You -- you understand, don't you, that -- let me rephrase that. Do you agree with me that the whole purpose of examining statistics relating to population movements, the whole purpose in the Tabeau reports for examining statistics for the population movements in the indictment municipalities and deaths in 1992 in the indictment municipalities, was to try and give this Trial Chamber some idea of what happened in the indictment municipalities? You -- in terms of migration and deaths. So that, from that, they can draw whatever inference they want as to the reasons for those movements and deaths. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I must explain. Statistics does not analyse these movements. It only provides numerical data. And the analysis is up to other disciplines. Statistics only provides numbers. And I said yesterday that a number can say whatever the one willing to play with it wants to. Ms. Tabeau's report -- or, rather, in her report, apart from a host of statistical data, I haven't noticed any deeper-going analysis about causal processes when it comes to demography, demographic processes. I think that would have been desirable, and that's why I tried to point it out in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor Pasalic. We agree entirely. In fact, I'd go further than you. I would put to you, I would suggest to you, that there's nothing in any of the -- in the two, the Milosevic report and the case-specific report relating to population movements, authored by Tabeau that deals with the reasons for movement. You agree with that? Nowhere. She doesn't put forth reasons why people moved. You agree, don't you? Unlike you.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I believe that a number, an isolated number, is not telling unless it's analysed. Numbers do not speak to us unless an analysis ensues out of which we can draw conclusions. That's what I stick to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Look, I'm not asking you about what numbers say to us. I'm asking you a simple question. You agree with me, don't you, that Ewa Tabeau in the two reports, the Milosevic and the case-specific report for this case, she never touched upon reasons why people moved. She just showed where people were living in 1991 and where they were in 1997, based on the OSCE voters registers. That's all she did; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. It was made that way, and I've already put forward a remark that it wasn't done correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You, on the other hand, claim to have this material that does provide reasons for movement, the research that you did in 1992 to 1995, why people moved or, in particular, why Serbs moved. So why didn't you analyse that, draw up your statistics, present them in your report, and come here and tell this Trial Chamber the reasons why people moved?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was of the opinion that the reasons are contained in these four integrated factors: political; economic; demographic, due to birth dates and mortality; as well as socio-psychological. That is some objective and subjective reasons. Stating each of these reasons individually would have required much more time. And in this case, I didn't have as much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. You -- in the Milosevic report, having read it, you'll know that the only -- the only study that Tabeau did of reasons for movement, if -- if -- let me withdraw that question. The only time that the Tabeau reports ever provide any suggestion as to reason for movements is the comparison that the author did of her Demographic Unit figures on final conclusions of IDPs, internally displaced persons in the indictment municipalities, with UNHCR and Bosnian government database numbers on refugees and internally displaced persons. Do you remember that part of the report? That's from the Milosevic report, I -- I should say.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I read it. I remember that she used the data for 1991, when the last census was, of course, and the most recent data, but not government data because there is no Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina - she probably means the Council of Ministers - and the data from UNHCR that registered things in Bosnia-Herzegovina and surrounding countries. But I also noticed that there are terminological mistakes. She mentioned the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but she probably means the Council of Ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can we get up on the screen page 47 of P1627. That's the Milosevic report. P1627. And in English -- sorry, in B/C/S, I think it's at page 52. It's section 3.5. I think Professor Pasalic should have the B/C/S ... or -- it's coming. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You see -- you can see in the first paragraph that the purpose of the study was to compare the Demographic Unit, the DU, that's Demographic Unit, statistics from the voters registers with the UNHCR statistics that they finalised in 2000. That's basically the -- called the DDPR Database. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in the next paragraph, you see that she compared absolute numbers, and by that I think we can safely assume we're talking about individuals, absolute numbers from the two sources and proved that the minimum numbers produced by the Demographic Unit for 1997/1998 based on the voters registers are generally lower for Muslims and Serbs than the official DDPR statistics for the year 2000. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have the text in front of me. I can see it. But there are many figures here. I don't know which paragraph you were reading from.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, my apologies. Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Third paragraph, you see that the database that she -- she compared her statistics with is the official registration system of internally displaced persons and refugees in Bosnia and Herzegovina established by the UNHCR and the government. And produces official statistics for municipalities, settlements, and other areas. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So that -- does that remind you of the exercise that she conducted basically, which was: Compare her statistics with official Bosnian government and UNHCR statistics on IDPs?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably the methodological principle applied by Ms. Tabeau. We can conclude as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And I think she comments that the comparison led to the conclusion that the Demographic Unit figures were basically conservative. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the last paragraph, if you're referring to that. But I don't see anything in there except for some statements with regard to these movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what you mean. The last paragraph that starts with the database was established by UNHCR ... et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps we can speed this up by just turning over the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please, and show Table 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. You see on the left-hand column are the OSCE figures; they're the figures produced by the Demographic Unit of the OTP, overall numbers. And the UNHCR government figures. And there's a lot in this section dealing with various checks and -- and -- and deficiencies and problems that she had to deal with in order to effectively compare the figures. But that's the end result there, in Table 10. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And so for the Milosevic case area, the Demographic Unit came up with 88.756 Serbs against 96.871 Serbs. Do you see that comparison? And the overall figures --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sorry. And the overall figures at the bottom are slightly more conservative. Total of IDPs at the bottom is slightly more conservative than the UNHCR figures. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the UNHCR registers refugees and IDPs, doesn't it, and it did so in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the years following the war?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could notice that in the sources that I used in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And the -- in order to get yourself registered as an IDP if you're a Serb or if you're a Muslim or Croat in Bosnia, or a refugee, you have to provide an explanation of what happened to you, such that you qualify as a refugee or an internally displaced person for UNHCR purposes; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that they had defined criteria for all persons to be registered as internally displaced. Or as refugees, if they left Bosnia-Herzegovina for third countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And on a practical level, they had to do that in order to give a person some -- whatever benefits they can acquire as -- as a refugee, payments and registers of where they came from and assist them to return to their areas and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those would be the reasons for collecting this data. Because here we're talking about collecting data. In statistics, there is the collection of data. It's ordering and analysing and publicising. This is the period of collecting data. Whether they are collected in the best possible manner is something we can't go into.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So in terms of reasons for movement, that's a pretty good comparison to make, isn't it, for Ms. Tabeau? Because her figures broadly match up with the figures held by the UNHCR as to IDPs. And the UNHCR is in a good position to know reasons for movement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that they did collect data. But I must be very honest and say that this methodology wasn't available to me, nor was I familiar with that. Nor do I know how accurate this data is. Here's why: It is obvious that some persons manipulated their registration and they tried to register at various places. It was very difficult to eliminate that. And the same thing happened with voters register. One and the same person could vote at several places, and then that gives a distorted image. It is questionable to what extent this register can be considered a relevant document for drawing conclusions. I have some reservations with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But apart from cases of individual fraud, it's -- it's -- it's a sensible approach, wouldn't you agree? If you say, Well, my conclusion is X number of IDPs from the indictment municipalities, based on simple fact of movement; then go and compare those numbers with UNHCR who does claim to know who really is a refugee and an internally displaced person; if they're the same, it would tend to point to the conclusion that the numbers measured by Ewa Tabeau were, in fact, numbers of internally displaced persons and refugees?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the statistical or mathematical point of view, that is all right. But from the practical point of view, I preserve the right to have my reservations because of fraud and mistakes made when calculating these figures. That is the difference. The approach itself is not wrong with -- if everything was done with good intention, and I don't doubt that, but I doubt the validity of the results. And that is not difficult to corroborate by analysing voters registers where one person appears in several registers. I'm not talking about individual events, but a rather widespread occurrence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's leave this topic now. Part of your report is the -- are the annexes, and Annexes A1 to A10 of your report are 71 pages long. And they are basically the fruit of your 1992-1995 researches; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the summary of my research on the ground. That is my empirical research. I used standardised forms such as questionnaires, polls, and interviews. Apart from that, I used the 1991 census as a source, which, at that time, was the most relevant source for some data. By combining these approaches, I arrived at the results I presented in tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Before we go into this in any more depth, I just want to know this: Is the material in these annexes, Annexes A, A1 to A10, are they important for your theory of territorial ethnic homogenisation, your position of territorial ethnic homogenisation?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This material, as well as the material of other authors, that is, Tabeau and the Research and Documentation Centre of Mr. Tokaca, all show the importance of the process of the ethnic territorial homogenisation for various reasons, which we can discuss, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Nowhere in your report could I see, could I find, any section telling us how to use them or what they establish. Did I miss something, or am I correct? Because I couldn't see anything in there. There's your report and then there's the annexes.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question correctly, that it's unclear how they should be used, I explained yesterday how the table is to be read and how the data should be understood. I can only repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose -- well, if that's not clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah. I certainly -- heard your evidence yesterday. No problem. But why didn't you include that in your report? It would have made it a lot easier for the reader, wouldn't it, to tell us what the meaning of Annexes A, and also B for that matter, how to approach them, how to read them, what their purpose is, and how precisely they assist conclusions that you make in your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have done that, of course. But I've already told you that I had limited time at my disposal for drafting this report. I believe that these figures and these tables are very clear for drawing conclusions from them. And I could have explained in a more comprehensive elaboration to make it clearer to the wider audience, but the expert audience understands the report as it stands. Let me explain. These data were collected and processed 15 or 16 years ago, that is, in 1996. And these are the original data in these tables. If I were to make new analyses now, I would probably recompose them and adapt them to some new processes that are underway now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, I don't know where you get -- why you move on to a discussion of new analyses. My question was really very, very simple: Is there any particular reason why you didn't help the reader by including in your report how Tables A1 to A10 should be used, how they should be read, what they are there for, what conclusions in your report they support? That's all. Nothing more than that. Is there any particular reason why you didn't include such explanations?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no reason but the shortage of time. I've already said that. Or possibly also considered it unnecessary because I supposed everybody would understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, you'd forgive the reader, wouldn't you, from looking at Annex B and thinking that those figures in -- sorry. Yes, in Annex B, in thinking that those figures relate to people rather than households. We didn't find out until yesterday that those statistics aren't people, they're households. You could have given us that sort of information, couldn't you? Make it a little -- just a little bit easier? After all, demographics is not an easy topic, is it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree. I could have pointed that out in a footnote and provided a brief explanation. That's probably a technical omission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's leave that and move on to the annexes themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could we get page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just intervene here because I raised this question with Professor Pasalic yesterday. And I think you said, Professor, that actually you were in possession of the number of persons, rather than the number of households which you have exhibited here. Are you able to provide these figures to the Chamber? And the reason I'm asking, of course, is that it would make your studies more comparable to other similar studies which we have seen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I think that I have that information here in my material, and I will be able to provide you with that, the number of refugees and displaced persons, and, on the other hand, the number of households. If you will allow me a moment, I will try to find it here in my material so that I can give you the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Professor, I suggest you find those figures during the next break, which is in 15 minutes. Then you will have 20 minutes to sort it out. Thank you very much. Back to you, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Didn't you say yesterday we can work out the figures on individuals; all we do is multiply a household by four. That's right, isn't it? That's what you said yesterday. That's the way to find out the figures, figures of individuals?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said at that moment, if it was unclear how many persons were involved, on average, it is multiplied by four, because that is the average number of household members according to the census in 1991. However, those are not official data. I do have official data though. So I can give you that so that we have the exact number of refugees and displaced persons, because that is from the list of refugees and displaced persons compiled in 1996. And that is the official material we use in our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So four is an average; is that right? Is that -- you use the average of four people per family, multiply the number of families, and, presto, you have the final figures of individuals; do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the average. But I repeat: In statistics, that is the greatest deception of all. Of course, I'm saying that by way of a joke. That is an average, of course, but there are deviations from one local community to another, depending on the density, the age of the population, the gender structure of the population, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. We'll maybe return to this later. Anyway, can we look at -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we look at page 19 of the annex, please. Page 19 in Annex -- that's annex A3 of Professor Pasalic's report. Page 19 in -- I think for e-court purposes it's English page 98 and B/C/S page 96, but I'm not sure about that. It's the figures for Pale. No, I'm sorry, I don't think that's the right one. It's page -- page 19 of Professor Pasalic's annexes. Oh, yes, it's there now, sorry. Thanks. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The -- you can see your figures now, Professor? And we're looking at Pale.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So for Pale, we've got two -- two settlements, Praca and Renovica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the figure of 16.310, is that the total, all people in the municipality, based in -- from 1991?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the figures in the first three columns - total population, total population of Serbs greater than 50 per cent, total population of Serbs under 50 per cent - they're all figures obtained from the census?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the next three columns, that's all the result of your researches?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If you look at burned or destroyed settlements for Pale, we've -- the correct way to read it is one destroyed settlement's a place called Praca, but Renovica wasn't destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's only the population that left Renovica. There were few of them anyway, at least at that point in time when I was conducting my research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But it -- these statistics don't show the extent of the destruction, of course. So it could be the entire settlement or it could be a barn.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Statistics don't show that. However, if a settlement was basically destroyed, then that information is entered here. However, if it is just a house or an auxiliary building that was destroyed, of course that is not recorded as the entire settlement. However, I provided explanations to that effect. Where only part of a settlement was destroyed, then we state that in parentheses. That is not what happened in this case, but you may have noted it in other cases. Also, it depended on what ethnic group populated part of the settlement involved or all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And it doesn't tell you when the destruction or partial destruction occurred or who caused the destruction or partial destruction either, does it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's impossible to state all of that in these tables. I've already explained that. On the basis of the patterns -- or, rather, in the forms in which all of this information was collected, all of that is stated. Even after the Dayton Agreement there was destruction of various settlements, and that was recorded. That would have to be a pile of documents that would have to be attached to this document. I did not think that that was relevant, that we had to give the dates and times involved in detail. I believed that this is the key information reflecting the processes taking place in the area. Who did it is quite obvious. This is the persecution of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But the information that I was talking about, namely, exactly how much destruction occurred or when the destruction occurred or who caused the destruction, was available to you from your 1992 to 1995 researches.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you not have enough time to put that information into this -- these tables, to analyse the information you had and then produce the statistics and introduce the statistics into your tables?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, it meant a shortage of time. However, I didn't really think it was all that necessary to go into such minute details. There is information available; I collected it myself on the ground, so I can interpret this information at any point in time. Of course, 15 or 20 years later I cannot recall each and every date, but I can work on the basis of annual reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the same considerations apply to execution sites, there, as well, don't they? No information as to when the execution occurred, how many people were killed, who was killed, who killed them?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this information exists in the forms that I filled out and collected. I repeat: On the basis of these individual forms, I then completed the picture as to everything that had happened in the area. I translated that into certain symbols used in tables. I explained yesterday that this cross, that is, a symbol for places where persons suffered, is actually a symbol of places where more than five persons were killed. That is an interpretation that was provided by legal people, and we even gave symbols for the places where we know the exact number of victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is this an appropriate moment, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose it is. So we will continue in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, Annex A, all the Annex As, only deal with Serbs, don't they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, could I just kick in a short question to the witness before we leave Annex A3, if that was your intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, no, I'm going to stay with the annexes generally, but, of course, I'm -- it doesn't bother me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Very quickly then. Professor Pasalic, in the table that we just saw before the break regarding Pale, you mentioned that Serbs were expelled from both of the two settlements that are included in this table; namely, Praca and Renovica. My question is: Do you know how many people, how many Serbs, were expelled from these two settlements? Was it all of the 1100 people or was it just a smaller number? Are you able to provide that additional information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That is contained in columns 2 and 3. 520 for Praca and 34 for Renovica. The total number is 554 inhabitants of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Professor, you may have misunderstood my question. In column 5, you indicate that Serbs were expelled from both settlements. And my question to you is: How many Serbs were expelled from these two settlements? Was it all of the 1102 people who were expelled or was it a smaller number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you haven't understood me. 1018 inhabitants is the total population of Praca, including 520 Serbs. The rest are of other ethnic backgrounds. Renovica had 84 inhabitants, 34 of which were Serbs. So Serbs, 520 in Praca and 34 in Renovica. They were expelled, all of them, making up a total of 554. The rest were not because they had different ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. And please forgive me for not having understood it. It was not completely clear. So when -- in these tables, when you indicate that Serbs have been expelled from the settlements or the villages, then we are to conclude that it was all of the Serbs who lived there who were expelled, in all settlements; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. Unless I pointed out somewhere that it has to do with parts of the population that was expelled. However, if there is no special note, that means everyone. Usually that is what happened. For the most part it would be one ethnic group that would be expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, just let's look at precisely what we've just been answering, because I think some further clarity could be put in here. The first three columns for Pale, I'm not talking about the town, but where it contains the figures 1018, 520, and then a blank. Do you see that? They're taken from the census figures. They are census figures, are they not?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... right. Right. Okay. Right.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yep, you have. You have indeed, thank you. The next three - burned or destroyed, settlements from which expelled, execution sites - that's all based on your figures; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That are based on standardised forms containing a series of data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... okay.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are archives that are stored in a particular place, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And before the break, you agreed with me, didn't you, that your figures don't explain, where you say that, for example, people are expelled, how many people were expelled?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that I've explained that. In individual documents or, rather, questionnaires or polls, that is contained there, and it is supplemented in my reports --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- as this one is, and the printed book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is just a particular magnitude provided in general figures, because it would require a great deal of material if we were to attach all of that. And that is usually not done in scholarly work. This is an archive that one usually refers to and that one represents in a particular paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And we're been through that earlier this morning, haven't we? So in that particular example for Praca and Renovica, if you look at the column, the second-to-last column, settlements from which Serbs were expelled, in the English translation there are two blanks, that means they're positive. In fact, in your report you say there's two symbols and that means yes, Serbs were expelled from those two -- two -- two places, Praca and Renovica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a purely technical material. That it was impossible to use the same symbols when the English translation was being done. I think that Mr. Cvijetic explained that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... he did --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a purely technical problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He did, indeed. So there's nothing to indicate, just from the fact that Serbs were expelled, that 520 people from Praca and 34 people, rather, Serbs, from Renovica were the numbers that were expelled. All you can say is that people were expelled, Serbs were expelled from those two particular villages in the municipality of Pale. Because to get the numbers, we have to go back to your information that you obtained in 1992 to 1995 because that's where it's all buried; right? Those figures of 520 and 34, they're just census figures of Serbs who were living there at the time, in 1991.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. What we present here are data from my book in which they were referred to. In such publications, it is impossible, and it's not right either, to provide each and every detail that concerns every person that was expelled from a particular settlement. However, I repeat: That is why archives exist about each and every individual case. In this case, it would have required thousands of pages attached to this publication. If we were to follow that logic, then we could ask for such data to be attached to Ms. Tabeau's report because I do not see information about each and every victim referred to in her report. So that is the way we should look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And you've mentioned that several times this morning. But my assessment is correct: In the section -- the column, settlements from which Serbs were expelled, there are no numbers. That's buried back in your material, you say. All that that column shows is that some Serbs, unknown number, on an unknown date were forced out of those two places by unknown perpetrators; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... excuse me, Your Honours, but we have already received an answer in response to Judge Harhoff's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I give an answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. Let's move on, please, to a question that I -- I wanted to start off with, and that's this: The study, of course, only relates to Serbs, Annex A; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yesterday in your evidence, sir, Mr. Cvijetic was asking you questions about chain reactions. And you said this: "As I have already pointed out," this at page 20526. "As I have already pointed out, it is necessary to emphasise the complexity of all the processes and movements in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the whole population. As we know, the population comprises of the three ethnic groups, three constituent peoples, as well as members of other peoples. If we study all this in a comprehensive way, we obtain a realistic and a comprehensive picture of all the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the demographic aspect that we are discussing today." So if we take what you said yesterday, your entire Annex A which only deals with Serbs must fail to do -- to provide what you call the realistic and comprehensive picture of movements in Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my responsibility to explain that. The question is a proper one, why I only deal with demographic processes involving only one ethnic group. I think that I've already explained that. During the war, that was -- there were restrictions. You could not study processes throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. You could only do it in areas where you could move about. So I was in an area where I could study demographic processes involving the Serb population. After the war, after a certain amount of time, the conditions became right for such research as well. However, Ms. Tabeau's research, as well as that of the IDC from Sarajevo, had already been rather all encompassing, so I believe that anything I would have done would have been duplication. I thought that all of this put together would have provided a more realistic and more comprehensive picture. That is where I see the significance of my own research, although it did not include all the demographic processes because that was impossible. Finally, I did not have the capacity to do that, to study a span of ten years. This is a lot of work, and to this day practically no one succeeded in doing that. However, if there are more of us involved, then we can give a more comprehensive picture and also a more realistic and impartial one, as is required in science. That is my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought you were about to ask a follow-up question, because there's a question that occurs to me arising out of his answer, and I don't ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Please, would Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Professor, having regard to the limitations that you've just articulated, what, then, may I ask, was the purpose of your doing the study at the time you did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that I was engaged to do research by the state documentation centre for war crimes research, the research of war crimes done against the Serbian People. And I'm convinced of the significance of this research, although it didn't cover the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which wasn't possible. So that now, in the post-war period, we may be able to get a comprehensive view of the demographic movements, including the works and research done by a number of authors and institutions. I believe that this is the basic purpose of my research. Because we could ask the question: If the centre had not done this research, would we, today, have data about a part of the population or an ethnic group that go into this level of detail for the period of 1992 through 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And while we're on this topic: You'd agree, from having read Ewa Tabeau's three basic records, Milosevic, the case-specific report, and war victims, those three, that throughout her reports, studies, an outstanding feature is the fact that there are comparison tables and analyses of all three ethnic groups from the indictment municipalities. You agree with that -- and you can -- proposition?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I noticed that there are such data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I put to you that regardless of whatever difficulties you may have had in obtaining materials, study materials, on the basis of your own words, your study is fatally flawed because of the failure to study the other two ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would, of course, have been much better if I had been in a position -- speaking from hindsight, if I could have studied all ethnic groups. Then I would have had a comprehensive study for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But it was impossible at the time. I can reply with a question: Why didn't any scientist from the Federation do such research covering all of Bosnia-Herzegovina and including all ethnic groups? Nobody did because it was practically impossible. We had these mechanisms and research to engage in such research for object or subjective reasons. But I considered this a step forward in the research of events in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time the events were happening. There is no better research. It could have been better if we had better mechanisms and work conditions. That is fairly obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I must remain with Annex A, but I want -- let me rephrase that. Yesterday, and I think again today, you've mentioned that -- that your study, which produced Annex A, had consisted of five years of research using standardised instruments, direct interviews -- direct research, sorry - interviews, polls, and personal insight. And that's what you said yesterday at transcript 20552. Why didn't you include your methodology in your report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't give a detailed description of my methodology in the report, but it is clear from the character of this work that this is empirical research, original, scientific research on the ground, which, in the classification of scientific research, is considered the most relevant research.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. But wouldn't you agree with me that if it is empirical, scientific, original research that the methods that you used to collect these statistics are possibly the most important thing to make clear in your -- in your report? In fact, it's basically just commonplace, isn't it, for statistical studies to -- to set out the methodology used?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it depends for what purpose you draft a report. Then you can describe the methodology and the methods. Because these are two different things. One thing is the methodology; the other thing are the methods. I didn't do so here because I considered it obvious from the results and from the information that the methods I applied were geographical maps, questionnaires, polls, inductive and deductive methods. I don't have to list them all. I didn't consider it necessary to list them in detail here, but I'm ready to explain which methodology and which scientific methods I used in this work. I must point out that what we're talking about in this annex was literally taken over from my printed publication. This is explained in the footnote. I didn't modify anything that was publicised in my monograph. I could have done so for the wider audience, but for the purposes of this report, I assumed that everybody who read it would understand what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And would understand what your methodology was in collating the statistics, even though there's not one word in your report about your methodology, they would understand that, too, from simply reading it; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But a selected audience. For the wider audience, it would not be as obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... all right --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My methodological approach was that of scientific research on the ground. And the scientific methods are the ones I mentioned. For the wider audience to understand the technical terms and terminology, because this is mostly dealt with at institutions of higher education, were the students who attend certain courses. For example, I teach the methodology of scientific research for social sciences at the post-graduate level. I do -- I teach at the University of East Sarajevo. So I don't believe that this is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave methodological research and go to one last aspect of Annex A. Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like to have up on the screen the tables for Novi Grad and Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you will see that it's in page 14 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I understand, for e-court purposes, in English it's page 98, and in B/C/S it's page 96. And it's part of A3.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. We've got it there. Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I hope you've got -- I can't read the Cyrillic, of course. I hope you've got Novi Grad and Novo Sarajevo in front of you. I see you nodding, so, yep. Good. We've already -- we know what these figures mean because we've touched upon Pale earlier. So Novi Grad, as part of the settlement that you looked at for Novi Grad, the municipality of Novi Grad is one settlement called "part of Sarajevo"; and in the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, you looked at another settlement within that municipality, and that's also called "part of Sarajevo." So they're just two settlements, two of several settlements, in both municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can try to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you don't mind --

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territorial organisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you don't mind, Professor Pasalic, I don't want an explanation. I just want to proceed through this as quickly as we can. Could you just tell me if I'm right or not right: Novi Grad has a settlement called "part of Sarajevo"; Novo Sarajevo has a settlement called "part of Sarajevo." Both of those two settlements are just one of several settlements in both municipalities; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a yes or no answer. Novi Grad is a municipality that's part of the city of Sarajevo. Novi Grad [as interpreted] is another. Parts of these settlements are territories where -- from which Serbs were expelled or settlements of which parts were destroyed and burned. It's not part of the settlement, but it was an area of the settlement where they were most concentrated. It -- these -- these are the areas where the population density is highest. So Sarajevo is more demanding from the point of view of research than other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we can cut through this. Let's get the 1995 published-by-Croatia census material from the 1991 BiH census. Sorry that was inelegantly put.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like to have 65 ter 1561 put up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And while that's coming up: Professor, you have next to you, or you brought with you, the 1991 Bosnia-Herzegovina census published by the Croatian authorities in Zagreb next to you on the desk, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not today, because I showed it yesterday. But I can see what we have on the screens. I didn't consider it necessary to bring it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm willing to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And you brought it for reference purposes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a source of data, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could we get up page 36 of this document. Yes, 36. Unfortunately, we have to -- the -- the material spreads across two pages, but we can try and quickly see how it's set out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the bottom, you see Novi Grad; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't see the year 1991. It's on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it sure is. It sure is. Just let me take you through it, and I think we can get through this fast, all right? The figures that you see at the bottom, in fact, are 1948, 1953, 1961, 1971 figures, but if you go -- but you can see there that in Novi Grad there are three settlements: Bojnik, Ricica, and Sarajevo Dio; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can we have page 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the material in this goes horizontally across the pages, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The following page contains the data for 1991. These are the relevant data in our example.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it possible to put two pages up there so we can see -- makes it easier; page 36 on the left hand, and page 37 on the right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. The figure on page 37, that's the total, isn't it? The word used is "ukupno," u-k-u-p-n-o. And that's total, isn't it, 136.616?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And then we have totals for Muslims -- sorry, for Croats, Muslims -- Muslims, and Serbs in the whole of Novi Grad; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yugoslavs and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if we look at these census figures, for Serbs we see that in the whole of Novi Grad, in the whole of Novi Grad, that's Novi Grad consisting of Bojnik, Ricica, and Sarajevo Dio, there are 37.591 Serbs.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And if you look at your table of Novi Grad, you say there are 50.000 Serbs in just one of those settlements, the settlement you call part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's why I say "part." Some Serbs remained in that settlement. They weren't expelled. It was populated by them, and it was controlled by other formations. It was difficult to delineate in such a very densely populated city. These were very complex matters, so it was difficult to be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: With respect, it's not complicated in the slightest, is it? The census figures show that in the entire municipality of Novi Grad, the entire municipality, there were 37.591 Serbs as at 1991. You say 50.000 Serbs in your -- in your table. That's a mighty discrepancy, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but we must clarify this. I state 50.000, not 15.000; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, we agree.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did this -- these 50.000 come from? Why aren't they 37.000? I disregard the categories Yugoslavs and others. According to our estimates, the greatest percentage of these were of Serb ethnicity, and they were expelled together with the Serb population. I must admit that this is an estimate. There are no more Yugoslavs, no such category in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And we proportionally divided them up between the three ethnic groups. Traditionally, the highest percentage of Serbs declared themselves as Yugoslavs, those who had a strong historic nostalgia for that state that was called Yugoslavia from 1918 on. But I agree, it was an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. So that's people who call themselves Serbs in the census and then people who called themselves Yugoslavs who were really, in fact, Serbs, according to you. And you added those two figures and you came up to a nice round figure of 50.000. That's what you did, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figure is round because it's an estimate. And without a census, it was difficult to obtain an exact figure, which probably wouldn't have been as round. So it's an estimate that most of these 15.000-odd [as interpreted] Yugoslavs are, in fact, Serbs. According to our estimates, that was obvious in Sarajevo, when it comes to these shares.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did it ever occur to you to put this into your tables? You know, this 50.000 Serbs who were in -- in these -- in Novi Grad were, in fact, people who declared themselves to be Serbs and people who declared themselves to be Yugoslav but who, as we all know, in fact, are Serbs. Did it ever occur to you to make that clear in your statistics?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I give a clearer explanation in the textual part. This is merely a table, a bare statistical figure. But in my monograph, I explain the proportion based on which we estimated the affiliations of the group called Yugoslavs. Whether that estimate is objective or subjective is, of course, open to discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What monograph? Where -- where in your report do you talk about the affiliations of Yugoslavs? Where in your report is there the slightest word that we can safely treat Yugoslavs as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote two monographs about wartime demographic processes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. One is the suffering of Serbs and Serb settlements from 1997, and the other is an amended edition titled "The Anthropogenic Reality of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina." These are the two monographs that are directly linked to these demographic processes, and the data can be found there. In this particular report, I didn't point this out, apart from the footnotes in the annexes, because the annexes in this report are basically scanned and it was impossible to amend them, and you see that they are in Cyrillic script because they are scanned. That's how it was done technically with my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. The -- you cite at the end of each of your annexes, from A1 to A10, the ethnic -- there's a source, being the ethnic composition of the BH population 1991 census, Belgrade, 1992. Couldn't you have just simply added the two figures that we see at page 37, Yugoslavs and Serbs, and put them together and come up with a precise number, rather than 50.000? I mean, you do cite the census.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't add them up because we didn't attribute all the Yugoslavs to the Serb group. It's our estimate that most Yugoslavs were actually Serbs who declared themselves Yugoslavs, and I explained why. It would been biased if I had simply added the Yugoslavs to the Serbs, arithmetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I'd like to tender the first page of that -- the Croatian-produced census figures for Bosnia-Herzegovina into evidence and these pages, in particular pages 36 and 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm trying to remember whether with the works of Ewa Tabeau possibly this was also admitted into evidence, so as to avoid duplication. Perhaps my learned friend can help me here. I believe that with the works, this very census to which both Ms. Tabeau and our expert witness are referring was also admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think it was, no. I don't think it was. I'm pretty safe in ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What should be looked at is whether the entire book was an annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think -- I'm certain it wasn't. I -- I've not been able to find it anywhere. And if Your Honours please, I'm more -- I'm happy for the book, the whole book, to go in if you wish, if you think that's preferable or if Mr. Cvijetic thinks that's preferable. I'm trying to confine the amount of material that we have in the system, so to speak. But I'm happy for it all to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would admit the tables, not the whole book. So that -- that would be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And can we just now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, just one moment, please. Professor, if -- so you are putting together the figures of Serbs and people who declared themselves Yugoslavs, or the greatest part of it. People who declared themselves Yugoslavs, they declare themselves not to be anything -- anything else, I suppose. So doesn't that -- to be able to do that, doesn't that -- don't you need a definition of Serb ethnicity? And doesn't that depend on what definition you give of Serb ethnicity? So I would ask: What is your definition of Serb ethnicity that enables you to include Yugoslavs into that category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you correctly, Serb ethnicity is defined on the basis of how one declared oneself at the last census in 1991. After the breakup of Yugoslavia, this category practically disappeared, that is to say, persons who declared themselves as Yugoslavs. It is proven that in neighbouring states they declared themselves in a different way, no longer as Yugoslavs. So let us make a comparison.
