In 1991, in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Serbia and in Croatia and in Slovenia and in all former Yugoslav republics, they declared themselves as Yugoslavs. The following censuses no longer contained that category of the population, those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs. It was logical, at least on a temporary basis, until the census we resort to estimates as to where that population group should go into. I tried to explain why we put most of them into the category of the Serb population, and I, indeed, believe that that is the case, knowing practical matters on the ground, where people lived, and what they declared themselves as after everything that had happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That can be shown by some other indicators as well: Like, refugees and displaced persons; they declared themselves as Serbs. That is evident from the 1996 census of displaced persons as refugees. Most of them are Yugoslavs -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because most of those who had declared themselves as Yugoslavs then declared themselves as Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Professor, can I just follow up on the question just put to you by Judge Delvoie by asking you if I have understood this table correctly in assuming that from Novi Grad and Novo Sarajevo all of Serbs who lived in these areas before the war were expelled from those areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As stated here, at the beginning of the war and further on, Sarajevo was a divided city, according to territorial units. In some parts, it was either one or the other ethnic group that prevailed. I mean Serbs and Muslims, because there was a negligible number of Croats before the outbreak of the war in Sarajevo anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's proceed to Annex B, please. Professor, what I'm not clear about is if this -- these -- the numbers in Annex B relate to Serb households only or whether they encompass all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Professor, I was just wondering about the answer that you just gave me, when you asserted that all of the Serbs registered in Novo Sarajevo and Novi Grad before the war were expelled during the war, that is to say, all together, 90.000 people from these two areas in the city of Sarajevo. Where do you have -- or where did you find the evidence that all of these people actually were expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, during expulsions in the territories where I conducted my research, we dealt with these persons directly by way of polls and questionnaires. Secondly, we had official data as to where they had temporarily moved after being displaced from that territory. For example, for example, the municipality of Pale, which had a population of 16.000 according to the 1991 census, now there is a population of almost 30.000. For example. We -- we registered that population in 1996 in all of those municipalities where they moved, and we came to these figures. However, we cannot always say that it was all of them. At least there is a statistical margin of error, that there was a significant minority of individuals who remained for a variety of reasons, mixed marriages, other family reasons, and so on. So this should not be taken literally, that all of them, to the very last one, had left a particular area. So basically the stronghold is the 1996 official statistics related to refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just to follow up on the line of questioning, and going back to Annex A, at page 19, in fact it's just underneath the section that we were dealing with for Pale. I don't think we need to bring it up on the screen, I can just read it out to you. You comment: "With the signing of the Dayton Accords, most of Serbian Sarajevo, Vogosca, Ilijas, Hadzici, Olovo, Sarajevo city zone went to the BH Federation, and the Serbian population had to move out of these areas which increases significantly the numbers of Serbs expelled from this territory." That's from your own report. Were those people included in these figures? The people who moved after Dayton, the Serbs who moved after Dayton.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you read my monograph carefully, then you see that I distinguish between these two categories. Serbs expelled until Dayton; and then Serbs from Sarajevo after Dayton. So the total is the final figure that was 830.000 [Realtime translation read in error "80.000"] displaced persons from the 1996 statistics. I could not have been as precise as a census process. I consider this census of displaced persons and refugees to be a very accurate instrument. So in response to your question: Yes, they were added to the Serbs who had left before Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a correction. It says "80.000," and I think that the professor said -- Say, once again, what was it that you said instead of 80.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The total number of Serbs who were refugees and displaced persons was 830.000 [Realtime translation read in error "83.000"]. That is obvious from the statistics concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you say it once again because again it is not recorded appropriately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The total number of displaced Serbs [Realtime transcript read in error "persons"] before and after Dayton is 830.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see why the interpreters don't want to record the number. I don't see what's wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We've given the right number every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Time pressures, Professor, so I'd like to move on to Annex B, please, and I'd like to look at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Di Fazio, just in order to -- to clarify what the witness said, I think, even in his second answer, the witness did say, and this is page 49, line 13, that he said the total number of displaced "Serbs" before and after Dayton is 830.000, just to be sure that it's recorded correctly. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Look at Annex B, please. It's at the very beginning of Annex B. It's in page 74 of the annex. I'm sorry, I don't have the B/C/S with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If the Court could assist in getting that up as well. It basically deals with municipalities of present residence, and the first one is Banja Luka. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you need the page references in the electronic version, I can provide them for you. I can help.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can't read Cyrillic, but I think we're there, aren't we? We have the B/C/S equivalents for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. These are -- you've -- you already explained it yesterday. This is -- on this page, we see the figures for Banja Luka. But there's a total written there, 132.298. That is a total for each of the municipalities. So Banja Luka, which is just underneath, you can see, 22.572, plus all the other municipalities through Annex B. Correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. These are households. 132.000 goes for all of Republika Srpska. And then there's a further differentiation in terms of municipalities from Banja Luka and further on. However, this has to do with the number of households, and I have prepared the figures concerning the number of inhabitants who were involved in the process of becoming refugees and displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. And ... forgive me, I can't remember what you said. Do these -- are these Serb-only households, or do they encompass all three groups?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see from this table, there is no differentiation according to ethnic affiliation. Quite simply, we record in the census all the inhabitants who moved into the area of Republika Srpska from their previous place of residence. However, for the most part, of course, these are ethnic Serbs from the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We can draw that conclusion on the basis of the number of Serbs who moved in from the Federation. However, it is quite certain that there are small numbers of members of other ethnic groups, either on account of mixed marriages or other factors that were present in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So your households in Annex B, probably mainly Serb, but could include Croat or Muslim households, but we've got no idea of what the numbers actually are.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know the figures, but we don't know of any differentiation according to ethnic group. I repeat: It is a negligible number of members of the Croat, Muslim, and other peoples. We can say quite freely that the absolutely dominant population that was moving out of the Federation was the Serb population. We can see from this information and other information, also from the other republics that are states today, outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that was clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I'm -- I'm not -- still not clear. I'm talking about all of the -- all of the figures that you include in Annex B, okay? For each municipality. Not just Banja Luka, okay? Talking generally about Annex B. We can't tell -- sorry. Does it deal in its entirety with mainly Serbs and negligible numbers of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it was primarily Serbs who had come from different areas. They came to all these different municipalities in the territory of Republika Srpska. Let us be quite clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. And basically what it shows is households that have moved. Because you've got a household of -- municipality of present residence for the household, and municipality of former residence for the household. So what these figures presumably seek to show is households that moved?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is clear from the heading of the table. So the municipality where they resided previously and the municipality that they moved into at the time of the census, which is called the present-day municipality or residence. That is why I repeat, for practical reasons, in order to regulate the status of these households, it has to do with all the members of the households, although there is information about all the persons who moved out and all other matters related to their structure. If necessary, I can present all that information here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, that won't be necessary. Can -- these figures are taken from the book of Marjana [sic] Spiric who wrote a book called "Population of Republika Srpska" from the -- and she's from the Faculty of Economics and the Faculty of Maths and Natural Sciences in Banja Luka; right? And I know where she got her data from, so there's no need to tell us about that. But you got the data that's in here from her book. I'm not asking you about where she got her data from.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we clarified the matter yesterday. All right. You're not interested, but they used information from the census, and I used data from their books as secondary sources because this information was taken from the list of displaced persons and refugees in 1996 as a primary source. And at that point in time, those were the most relevant books that dealt with this subject matter. Also, this came from the professors who were the most relevant. Professor Marjanac was my teacher and professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you check her figures from the book, the figures that are reproduced here?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 132.280 households is the equivalent of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpret did not catch the other number.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- 50.5 per cent of them are women, and 49.5 per cent are men. And, of course, there is ample data that I can provide in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment please, Professor. That is because of the rush, you always rush through all of this, the number of inhabitants was not recorded. There was the equivalent of the number of households. That would also be a response to Judge Harhoff's question, so would you say that slowly so that it can be recorded properly. And do look at the transcript that you see on your left-hand side, and you can see that there is a number missing and then perhaps you should do something about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I repeat. The total number of displaced persons and refugees as households is 132.298. And that is the equivalent of 419.879 individuals, categorised according to gender and age groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you're referring to her book, as we speak. You've got it open in front of you. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my monograph. But it refers to the source, Marjanac, this book that I also have before me. I have a copy of that book before me. I have both sources in front of me. I used data from the book Zdravko Marjanac or, rather, his paper on displaced, expelled persons and refugees. This is below my table. But, of course, you cannot see it now. However, you do have that book attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the -- Annex B is divided up in two parts. The second part, what you've done is to use the same figures but reverse the presentation so that instead of showing the municipality of present residence, it shows municipality of former residence first and then municipality of present residence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just put in a small question once again. Professor Pasalic, in the page which we are currently having on the screen, which shows a table of number of households that moved from various municipalities to the municipality of Banja Luka, then in the third column, on the top, you have Banja Luka appearing there with a number of 287 households that moved from Banja Luka to Banja Luka. How is that to be understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I explained that yesterday, and I thought it was clear. Within the boundaries of the municipality of Banja Luka, the population moved for a variety of reasons. That is to say, from a particular settlement, say, Zmijanje, they moved into the city of Banja Luka. We clarified that yesterday. I don't think there was anything unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that that was in response to His Honour Judge Delvoie's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise. I may have missed that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it time, Your Honours? I think it might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, just spot on. So we resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Annex B is divided into two sections. The first part shows municipality of present residence and then -- and then -- and the number of people in that present municipality, and then the municipalities where they came from. And it's just reversed in the second part of Annex B.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that's how it's presented in the tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I -- it may not be necessary to bring it up on the screen, but included in all of these statistics in the first part of Annex B are people who came from outside of Bosnia, from Slovenia, from Zadar, from Serbia, Zagreb, Macedonia, and so on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It can be seen in the tables that these are data collected in the census, and they are interpreted this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was it your idea to, for the second part of Annex B, to be a reversal of presentation, or was it the authors' idea to have a reversal of presentation; namely, municipality of earlier residence and then municipality of current residence?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my idea. I took it over from the authors mentioned, in its original form.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you haven't had a chance to -- well, let me withdraw that. You didn't check the figures yourself?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no need. Because they are based on the census. We're talking about official date from official institutions. I don't consider myself competent to verify them, because what could I change there anyway?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I -- okay. For the -- this reversal, and yesterday you called it, I think, inversion, or a countertendency. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because these are the headings of the tables. Flows and counter-flows of migrational movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I thought the inversion was the reversal of presentation of the same material, simply flipping it backwards. Instead of showing current residence -- present residence first and then municipality of former residence, it was shown by municipality of former residence first and then followed by municipality of present residence. You know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can explain, the municipality of current residence is Banja Luka. And then it is stated from which municipalities of former residence these people moved to Banja Luka. And the second part says municipality of former residence, Banja Luka, and then we see to which municipalities some households moved from Banja Luka. These are not the same households. They are different. And, of course, the figures are different, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, they're not. If you look at page 111, where we start from the reversal, municipality of earlier residence followed by municipality of current residence, you got the same figure, 132.298. Do you see that? Exactly the same figure. That's exactly the same total. So you're wrong.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking about different numbers for individual municipalities. But, of course, these are contained in the total of 132.298. We agree that this is the total. But by municipalities, 22.000-something moved into Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and a different number moved out of Banja Luka. Whereas, the total number of households is 132.298.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, could the professor just repeat the last part of his answer concerning Banja Luka because it was not recorded. You mentioned different numbers. Please tell us which different numbers these are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I repeat. The numbers are different. From their earlier residence, 22.572 households moved into Banja Luka. And -- and from Banja Luka, significantly fewer moved out. We cannot see the exact number, but it's about 400 households. However, both numbers are included in the total of the refugees and displaced persons, which is 132.298.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I -- I -- I'm sorry to persist, I just want the answer to a really simple question. It's really simple. And I ask you, Professor, to listen carefully, and I'll put it to you again. The first part of Annex B shows municipality of present residence total and then where those households came from, okay? And if you add up each and every municipality, using that method of presentation, you come up to -- what's written here is a figure of 132.298; page 74. Now, from everything that you've said and from the document itself, it's obvious that Annex B flips around its presentation. Now we start to look at municipality of earlier residence, the total in that municipality, and then the municipality of the current residence. And the figure is exactly the same, 132.298. And you can see that at page 111 of Annex B. Exactly the same figures. Correct? And I'm sure can you answer that with a yes or a no. I'm sure you can.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see these figures now. But I can say that the total number of displaced households and refugee households is 132.298. That's the final figure according to the 1996 census. The data cannot differ from this number. Only, different methodologies were used to break them down by municipality and the status or -- of the previous residence. But the total is always the same. It must be the same. 132.298.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Professor, I just want to put a proposition to you, because I'm afraid we just don't have enough time to go into this in the sort of detail I had envisaged. I put to you that this is the situation with your Annex B: The figure of 132.298 is the total of households for all municipalities in the first part of Annex B, but that includes -- and it shows municipalities of former residences as well; and, therefore, that part of the annex includes people who came in out of Bosnia. The second part, where the presentation is reversed, only includes Bosnian municipalities. Only includes Bosnian municipalities. It doesn't include, where it says "municipality of earlier residence," for example, Macedonia, or Zagreb. It doesn't include those people. So the reversal in Annex B is not actually a reversal because part of it's missing. And I put to you that if you add up all of the municipalities in the second part of Annex B, you come to a total of 76.836 households, not 132.298, as is mentioned there. And that's all I want to say about Annex B. I know you can't do the maths, but do you agree with the basic method of -- that I suggest should be used in looking at Annex B?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that municipalities and settlements outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina are also mentioned, if we look at my report. But I agree that possibly technical errors were made when adding them up. I can see Otocac, Pag, Pakrac, Pag, Petrinja, Pazin, and so on. You may have been able to see that in the second part of this annexed table.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. That's enough about Annex B for now. Let's move on to another issue, and that is sources. You had a lot to say about the census from 1991 in your report. You -- you say that it was never verified. The processed data was never published. And you, in particular, you -- you comment on the absurdity of Croatia publishing the results. And this is at paragraph 215 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In English, it's page 58; and in B/C/S it's page 58. Could We have that up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, this -- okay. Thank you. Good. Now this paragraph, 215, comes in your part of your report which is a commentary on the Prosecution's expert report by Ewa Tabeau et al. And then appears paragraph 215. And you say there that the 1995 State Bureau of Statistics printed this publication which was absurd. "The result of a population census to be printed and published in another country!" If it's absurd, why did you bring it and use it as a reference here in court?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it is absurd but not incorrect. It is absurd to carry out a census in one country and then to have those data published by a different country. That's the absurdity from that point of view. As for the accuracy of the figures, they are not being brought into question. However, I would like to direct you to Annex 214 where Nora Selimovic, an official from the Statistics Bureau of Bosnia-Herzegovina, confirmed my data that the 1991 data were never -- census were never verified. I quoted her in paragraph 217, and that is from Ms. Tabeau's report. Should I read that out? The quotation ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry, would Your Honours just give me one small moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. I'm with you now. Yes, you can see that in paragraph 217, your quote. Of course, that comment is taken out of context, isn't it? Because, first of all, Nora Selimovic is, in that part of the report, talking about controls of the -- and logical controls in the census, and she was there talking about the data that concerned dwellings and agricultural farms not being published because it hadn't passed the phase of logical control. So it was only data that dealt with dwellings and agricultural farms. In fact, you make that clear in your own report; right?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I really wish to describe that in an unambiguous way. Paragraph 216 says that it was only in 1998 that the Federal Bureau of Statistics printed the statistical yearbook presenting all the data from the 1991 population census in BH. As for Ms. Tabeau's report, it uses the age structure of the population to calculate certain data in respect of the persons born before 1980. They could not have had that from the census of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the publications that were published after 1991. It was only in 1998 that this yearbook appeared, and that is what Nora Selimovic speaks of. And, of course, also the census of households and so on. What is relevant here is what -- what refers to the population, its structure. That was not published until 1998, and that is stated clearly. Because that census had never been verified. It is verified by the National Assembly or, rather the Assembly of the then Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is the essence. It was never verified. And that is clearly acknowledged here by an official from the statistics bureau, and I just quoted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If you read paragraphs 214 through to 217, they're essentially a criticism of the use of the 1991 population census data basically because, you say, it's never been verified. And we'll get into that later. But -- and then in paragraph 217, you quote Nora Selimovic, who wrote that part of the Milosevic report, to corroborate your assertions. And you put that quote in that you can see, starting: "With the aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992, the processing of the census data ceased ..." And going on to end: "... the data on dwellings and agricultural farms were not published because this material never passed the phase of logical control." So you read the report, didn't you, and you plucked that quote from what Ms. Selimovic had written into her report to -- to establish -- to corroborate your criticisms of the census; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is absolute that we have reservations in our research when using data from the 1991 census because it was not fully published. Apart from that, a census being so comprehensive has to be ultimately verified in order to attain its final form. Although we use it, it never attained its official form. I used it and I corroborated it by quotes from the official of the statistics bureau of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I think that that is proper because the results of that census were not published until 1998. Further on, I think that information about farms was not published either because that had not gone through a logical check, so the conclusion is that the 1991 census has not fully been processed. That is why we refer to the previous census that had met all the requirements concerning census verification, and that was from 1981. However, that is something that happened a long time ago, so the information is no longer truly relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you took that quote from the Milosevic report of Ms. Selimovic, did you read three paragraphs down from where it appears, where she says, "The official data published on the population has passed all control phases including the control for duplicates that was conducted on the level of each municipality"? Did you read that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I have read it. Of course, new knowledge annuls the old, but I assert that census information from 1991 has only partly been published, and that is the number and the age structure. And that is done a month after the actual data-taking. All the other data is compiled and processed for a number of years. Because of the war situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that was impossible all the way up until 1998. Whatever Nora Selimovic, this official, wrote, the facts are as I have put them to you. If she has this verification to show, then I am prepared to withdraw what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All of this discussion concerning the use of the census by Ms. Tabeau and its reliability as a source is somewhat besides the point for this reason, isn't it? Ms. Tabeau used raw data that she obtained from the census, from the exercise of the census being conducted, to compile her statistics. She didn't just go to the census publications and pluck it from there. You understand that, don't you? And by "raw data," I mean individual-level data: name of a person, personal identification number, where they live. That's the raw data that was obtained by the census takers as they knocked on people's doors and filled out their questionnaires. And that's the data that she used. You understand that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed in her report that it had do to with such data and their comparisons. However, I still keep this reservation for 1997 and 1998 and the way in which this estimate was obtained. I explained that using some examples yesterday. We can repeat it today as well. I have no doubt that she had an opportunity to receive individual data, questionnaires of individuals, although that is protected information in our part of the world, I could not receive it in any way. This is strictly confidential. It is not made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you saying that you were denied the access to the same materials used by Ewa Tabeau for her studies, that you couldn't get access to it?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I cannot have access to individual questionnaires that the population filled out during the census. That is an operation that goes on for 15 days when people go from door to door. Because the data is protected by law for each and every person individually. I am not going into the way in which Ms. Tabeau obtained that data.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not interested in going into the way she obtained the data, nor am I interested in the legal protections. And I fully understand that data about persons, individuals, is confidential. I'm not asking you about any of those issues whatsoever. I'll repeat the question: Are you saying that you couldn't have gained access to the same date that she used? And I suggest you could have by saying to the -- those who told you to prepare this report, I need to see the same data that she used to prepare her reports. Simple as that.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible that on that occasion I could have asked for that, but, you see, I would have needed ten years, which is the amount of time that Ms. Tabeau used. And I am working, for, say, 100 hours. I used information about the census and I used other information apart from the census, just as Ms. Tabeau did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. But one thing's for sure: All of your criticisms about the census, whether they be true or not, are really irrelevant, aren't they, because you haven't looked at the data that she used, the raw data that was obtained from the census?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is not relevant whether I looked at it or not. I provided a critical review here, in terms of how somebody else did it. In this case, it was Ms. Tabeau. That is why I think that the data is irrelevant because it is not complete from the point of view of the census. I don't know whether anyone can assure me that she had each and every questionnaire and each and every document of 4.400.000 persons. If that was the case, it would have been a job that would have entailed years and years. However, the fact is that on the basis of this information, some other results were calculated, which, to my mind, and according to my calculation here, were wrong. And these are the so-called qualitative features of the population that were not published and processed officially, in terms of the age structure of the population, especially in that part of Ms. Tabeau's part -- report that deals with the population born before 1980. And I challenge that part of her report. I'm saying it's not reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Look, other sources of data that were criticised by you include the voters registers, the OSCE voters registers. You say they had many deficiencies. And I'm looking at paragraph 219 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So perhaps we can get that up on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. You deal with it there quickly in two paragraphs, 219 and 220. You say that they've got deficiencies, they're not suitable, and you say that it's a sample. And your main criticism seems to be that it's a sample of the post-war population and, therefore, not reliable. Do you see all that?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In paragraph 219, I commented on the unreliability of these voters registers, and then I quoted Ms. Tabeau's report. So I'm quoting from her report. She says the registration to vote was voluntary, which implies that the register is only a sample of the post-war population "... excluding those who did not register to vote because they were not interested, ill, too young, or too old ..." I agree that for those reasons these voters registers are not fully valid, and I also add here that there were duplicates of names on voters' registers in different places of residence. All of that together leads me to the conclusion that this voters register cannot be valid for drawing very important conclusions that are made in the report of Tabeau and others. So this is justified criticism. However, it is possible that she did not have a better mechanism that was available. However, it has to be criticised rightly because the accuracy of these data can be brought into question, and, after all, she recognised that herself, she admitted that herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So the basic criticism is twofold: The data itself is no good because it's got duplicates; and secondly, because it's only voters who registered to vote, it's a sample only and, therefore, is not of much use in -- in analysing migration movements. The whole sample of her study is to small. People who registered to vote, compared with those same people in 1991.

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is pointed out here is sufficient, namely that registering to vote was voluntarily. And voluntarily means the opposite of mandatory. So one thing is -- was what was collected as data in the 1991 census, and another, what was registered in this process. Of course, you must be -- must have your reservations and your doubts about data collected in this manner, the more so since the author herself admits that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You read what she wrote about the size of the sample that was obtained after she'd extracted the voters register, the statistics from the voters register. And that -- did you -- did you read that part -- part of the Milosevic report?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read those reports, but of course I don't remember everything. We would have to go back to those reports and analyse them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, let's see if we can do that in -- very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could we have page 219 up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I'd ask that you listen to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't know what the B/C/S is for 219. Sorry, I do have it. It's B/C/S page 59; and the English, it's page 59. Not paragraph 219, page 219 of the Milosevic report. I'm sorry. Which is P1627. E-court page 222, I'm told. And page 235 in B/C/S. Perhaps we don't need to proceed with that. I'll deal with this issue in this way because I'd like to move on, if we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the Milosevic report, Ewa Tabeau refers to the records that she got out of the OSCE voters registers. And from that she says that she got a joint database of 2.674.506 records. And out of that 2.6 million, she matched 2.13 million -- 2. - yes, we've got it up now - yeah, 2.13 million - yes, we've got it up on the screen now - 2.13 million with the 1991 census, and that's a matching rate of some 79 per cent. And I think you can see that in the B/C/S. And then she talks about problems that she encountered and how she dealt with them. And then she says in the -- further down that the total population of the country is 4.3 million. And the 1995 World Population Prospects gave another figure. But then she goes on to say: "It's clear that the 2.13 million voters constitute a large and reliable sample of the 18-plus population. Its size is big enough to prevent errors related to persons not registering to vote." She dealt there in some detail with the complaint that you make in your report at paragraph 219. Did you not consider looking at that part of her report, the Milosevic report, and attacking what she says there, rather than simply saying, Sample is not big enough?

utterances.speaker: STEVO PASALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have looked at this too, but it was sufficient to show it explicitly using that example. I can also state some objective complaints here. Who is it that found out that Bosnia-Herzegovina, in 1995, had 3.54 million inhabitants while the war was still raging? And there is also a forecast for the world population until 1998. We didn't have any idea of the development of the total population. This is very unreliable. I don't doubt the matching of this number of inhabitants. She's using unreliable data to derive conclusions from, estimated data, without stating a foundation for these estimates. If we're to confirm that Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1995 had 3 million inhabitants, could anybody prove that wrong? Or this figure here, 3.4 million. I consider everything put forward here rather unreliable. I respect the efforts made by whoever calculated this. But I said yesterday that this isn't only about mathematics and statistics; these are serious processes and live people. It was impossible to arrive at these results mathematically or statistically. If that had been so easy, we wouldn't have waited for a population census 20 years [as interpreted]. Even today, in peacetime, we don't know the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. How could we have known in 1995 that there were 3.54 million? To my mind, this is somewhat absurd. That is why I'm criticizing these data. If I could have offered accurate results, I would have done so. But I have pointed out this as a problem which still lingers in Bosnia. We don't know the population. We don't know its structure. And these are the most important indicators for all development programmes and other programmes, and this is still burdening us even today, in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks, Professor. It's for some relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand, at 1.30, that matters need to be discussed, unrelated matters. Or at least I was told by Defence counsel that they would like to address you at 1.30 on some issues relating to next week. I hope I haven't got that wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I confess, I hadn't heard that. But is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Yes, we have agreed that we need to address the Trial Chamber about the certain developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your Honours -- oh. I still haven't finished, and I think I've still got a bit more time left to me. Would now be an appropriate time for me to stop this? Because I'm moving into an area that's not strictly related to numbers, although I will have to return briefly to numbers at one later point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So upon the resumption tomorrow, how much longer do you think you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think I'll probably be about another three quarters of an hour, possibly an hour tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And re-direct, I suppose, would take an equivalent amount of time tomorrow. But we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, certainly no more than half an hour, possibly less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Professor Pasalic, we are not about to rise for the day, but as you would have heard from the exchange between counsel and the Bench, there are, as happens from time to time, certain procedural matters which the Court must deal with before it rises. So you are now going to be excused for the day, but the Court will not be rising at this point, so the usher will see you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was my understanding that this would -- this is going to be a joint submission by my friends from the Office of the Prosecutor, but they obviously gave me the floor. This is the situation we wanted Your Honours to be aware of: The day before yesterday we received the documents requested by Ms. Korner from Witness Bjelosevic. Among other documents, for the first time, I must admit, and it wasn't -- I wasn't aware of that fact, is that -- that there exists a diary of Mr. Bjelosevic from 1991 and 1992. I reviewed the diary yesterday and in the course of this morning, and I don't see any problem with -- with that document, nor the other documents. If the witness confirms that is his diary, there is obviously nothing for us to -- to say about that. However, I understand that the Office of the Prosecutor is experiencing a difficulty because of the diaries are written, of course, in Serbian, and they need to translate them. We discussed yesterday, and I gave what I could, my suggestions, to the dates which I think are relevant and the parts of the diary that -- that seem -- that seem to me to be relevant for this case and for the cross-examination of -- of Office of the Prosecutor of the witness Bjelosevic, as, of course, I can anticipate at this point. Now, we have agreed also that we will file a joint request to the CLSS to speed up the -- the -- the translation of -- of these documents. This is, -- Your Honours, the entries are perhaps one -- one page or a page and a half, two pages maximum long, and it's written by hand. So, therefore, it shouldn't be such an enormous burden for CLSS to at least draft translate these documents. My latest information - and I believe Mr. Hannis is here, he can confirm that. My latest information is that the Office of the Prosecutor -- well, unfortunate situation is that Ms. Korner is -- is -- was yesterday interviewing one of the -- the Defence witnesses and is only due to return to The Hague today, this afternoon. Now -- but what I understand the situation to be is that Ms. Korner would like to start the cross-examination and perhaps, in the course of the week, because her cross-examination of Witness Bjelosevic is anticipated to last four or five days even, that in the course of the week the translations will be available for her to cross-examine the witness, on the -- on the contents of the diary of the -- of -- of Mr. Bjelosevic. Now, Mr. Hannis will, I hope, confirm what I just said. This is the latest information that I -- that I have from the Office of the Prosecutor. Your Honours will remember that I -- that I inquired the day before yesterday about the date of return of Witness Bjelosevic, and the suggestion by the Trial Chamber was that he returns on Monday. Now we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On Monday with a view to resuming on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now we are in a better position to assess now the situation, and I would like -- I would like an advice from the Trial Chamber whether the situation is -- stays at the same, that the Witness Bjelosevic returns on Monday morning, because I have to inform the VWS about the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, these diaries which, as I understand it, are new, the pages which you have indicated may be relevant, in other words, we aren't dealing with a diary about walks in the woods or visits to the seashore, the question is, having regard to experience with backup log-jams from time to time in CLSS, do I - and it probably is a question I should pose to Mr. Hannis - but do I understand you correctly that the OTP would wish to have this material translated before they embark on their cross-examination? I'm not unmindful of what you said, that they could start in the hope that the translations would come on in the course of the week. But having regard to our past experience in this matter, I'm wondering whether -- and here the OTP can pitch in as to whether they would wish to begin if they aren't sure that they would have this material. How many page -- is there an agreement as to how many relevant pages we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, of course, I gave my assessment of the relevant dates that need to be. In my opinion, it's 20, 25 pages altogether. But it's a small diary, so the pages are actually half of the normal page. And it's written by hand, so it's relatively short.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me advise you of the information I have from Ms. Pidwell who's been speaking with Ms. Korner and been dealing with our language assistant who's been looking at the documents. It's my understanding the diaries -- I think there are three separate diaries totalling about 280 pages, handwritten pages. The initial assessment, I guess, by our analyst is that we might need something in the neighbourhood of 35 to 50 of those entries. Now, I don't know if an entry is one page, one paragraph, one sentence; I'm not sure what that is. But 35 to 50 handwritten entries. In addition to the diaries, though, we received in this collection of the documents something in the neighbourhood about 250 documents related to it. Now, our initial view of that is that we only need about 20 of those to be translated. In spite of all that, at the moment it appears that Ms. Korner would be ready and willing to start cross-examination on Tuesday, assuming, hopefully, that based on an urgent request to CLSS we can get a quick translation of those portions, the 35 to 50 diary entries and the 20 smallish documents, within a fairly short turnaround. She would like to start on Tuesday and then if it comes to pass that she hasn't been able, during our out-of-court time, to get those translations, review them, assess them, and figure out when to examine them, that there may be a request from the OTP on Wednesday or Thursday next week to have an additional day of recess or something to deal with those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the position is that we proceed, as anticipated, on Tuesday, and we will -- at some point in mid-week there would be an assessment or reassessment of the -- this new material and we see where we go from there. But practically speaking, there's nothing further that we can or need do at this stage. Is -- do I summarise the position correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, Your Honour. The only thing that would change that from our side would be if we learn from CLSS later today, they say, We can't do these translations for another ten days. That might change the position. But other than that, I think that's where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, of course, today being Thursday, if you should discover this before we rise tomorrow, you would alert us as to where we are. Thank you. Was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of these circumstances, this these diary is pretty relevant for my part of cross-examination related to the topic which I raised during the cross-examination with Witness Bjelosevic. So I would kindly ask Trial Chamber to allow me 30 minutes for additional cross-examination directly related to this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, could you remind me as to whether this witness is one where the Prosecution, in fact, started it's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour. That is my recollection as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In light of what Mr. Krgovic said, though, however, I don't know what Ms. Korner's position would be. If it were me, I would say, Well, I want him to do his cross-examination first before I continue any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to say that in the absence of any rule to the contrary, that's the obvious course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any problem. But we still need translation of this diary for my cross-examination. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krgovic can read Serbian. He doesn't need the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, that's all we can do for now. We'll see what the position is in the -- between tomorrow and Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 13th day of May, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.37 p.m.,
